summary: Extends MPLS LSP Ping and Traceroute (RFC 8029) so they can discover and exercise specific paths over Layer 2 ECMP across Link Aggregation Group interfaces. It also defines a way to learn the capabilities of a Label Switching Router. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: When several wires act as one, a test message might only travel along one. This lets testers check each wire separately.

subtitle: Teaching MPLS ping and traceroute to test every member link of a bundled link, not just the one a test packet happens to pick.

tldr.problem: MPLS LSP Ping and Traceroute were not designed to discover and exercise specific paths over a Link Aggregation Group, so a test message can be load-balanced onto a healthy member link and miss a broken one.
tldr.mechanism: The initiator sets a new G flag in the DDMAP TLV, and the responder describes each LAG member link separately with interface index and multipath information; a new LSR Capability TLV lets the two sides discover what is supported.
tldr.outcome: Operators get deterministic diagnostic coverage of each LAG member link. The RFC is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 8029 and has itself been updated by RFC 9041.

facts.label: Detailed Interface and Label Stack TLV

today: RFC 8611 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 8029, and it is itself updated by RFC 9041; it has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: The LAG Blind Spot
sections.content:
MPLS LSP Ping and Traceroute (RFC 8029) are designed to diagnose all available Layer 3 paths of a Label Switched Path (LSP), including Layer 3 Equal-Cost Multipath (ECMP). But Link Aggregation Groups (LAGs), defined in IEEE 802.1AX, provide Layer 2 ECMP, and the existing tools were not designed to discover and exercise those specific paths.

That leaves a gap. Label switching may work over some member links of a LAG but fail over others, and an MPLS echo request may be load-balanced onto a member link that works. The ping then succeeds and the label-switching failure of the bad member link goes unnoticed.

RFC 8611 extends the tools to give deterministic diagnostic coverage of LAG interfaces. The RFC says the work was motivated by issues encountered in live networks.
sections.eli5: Imagine four lanes on a bridge and one is closed. If your test car always happens to pick an open lane, you never learn that one lane is closed.

sections.title: How the Solution Fits Together
sections.content:
The solution adds a new LSR Capability TLV for discovering what a responder supports, plus extensions that describe multipath information for individual LAG member links. The reader is expected to know the Downstream Detailed Mapping TLV (DDMAP) from RFC 8029.

The initiator sends an MPLS echo request with a DDMAP TLV and the LSR Capability TLV, indicating that separate load-balancing information for each L2 next hop is wanted. The responder returns the same capability TLV as acknowledgement and adds, for each downstream LAG member, load-balancing information: multipath information and an interface index.

The RFC gives an LDP example. When node A runs LSP Traceroute toward node E, node B returns four entries: C over the non-LAG path, the first and second downstream C over the LAG, and D over the non-LAG path. The mechanism applies to all types of LSPs that can traverse LAG interfaces, and it does not change scenarios where an LSP is pinned to one particular LAG member.
sections.eli5: Instead of one answer for the whole bundle, each wire in the bundle now answers separately, so the tester knows which test message to send down which wire.

sections.title: Discovering What the Other Router Supports
sections.content:
Over the years many extensions have been added to MPLS Ping and Traceroute, so an initiator often needs to tell apart a responder that lacks a feature from one that simply replied without it. The LSR Capability TLV solves this. The initiator includes it in the echo request; a responder that knows it MUST include it in the echo reply, describing the features and extensions it supports.

A responder that does not understand the TLV replies with the return code "One or more of the TLVs was not understood", and the initiator can retry without it. It is RECOMMENDED that implementations of these LAG extensions include the TLV in their echo requests. A message MUST NOT carry more than one LSR Capability TLV.

The TLV has Type 4 and Length 4, followed by 4 octets of flags. This document defines two:

  • D, Downstream LAG Info Accommodation: the LSR can describe LAG member links in the Local Interface Index and Multipath Data sub-TLVs of the DDMAP TLV.
  • U, Upstream LAG Info Accommodation: the LSR can describe a LAG member link in the Incoming Interface Index sub-TLV.

Both flags MUST be cleared in an echo request. In a reply, zero, one or both MAY be set.
sections.eli5: Before asking a detailed question, the tester asks 'do you even know how to answer this?' The other router replies with a checklist of what it can do.

sections.title: Discovering the Paths Over a LAG
sections.content:
Once the initiator knows the responder can describe LAG member links, it sends an echo request with a DDMAP TLV whose new G flag (LAG Description Indicator) is set. The G flag is bit number 3 in the DS Flags field. In a reply, the responder MUST set G if a DDMAP TLV describes a LAG interface and clear it otherwise.

For each downstream interface that is a LAG, the responder MUST return a single DDMAP TLV, with the member links described by sub-TLVs. For each member link it MUST add a Local Interface Index Sub-TLV (with the LAG Member Link Indicator flag set) and a Multipath Data Sub-TLV, and it MAY add a Remote Interface Index Sub-TLV for the incoming link on the downstream router. The sub-TLVs for each link must stay together in that order, in order of increasing local interface index. If no received multipath information maps to a member link, its Multipath Length field is set to zero.

On the next hop (TTL=n+1), the initiator must update the DDMAP it sends over a particular member link: it removes the Local Interface Index sub-TLVs, keeps only the Remote Interface Index sub-TLV for the link being traversed (SHOULD), and reduces the multipath data to a single Multipath Data Sub-TLV.
sections.eli5: The tester says 'tell me about every wire'. The router lists each wire with its own number and the kinds of test messages that will use it.

sections.title: Checking That Each Link Was Really Used
sections.content:
The RFC defines two ways to validate that the member links were actually traversed. The first is used when the downstream router does not return Remote Interface Index sub-TLVs, which is common because that information is often not available on the responder. The initiator sets both the Interface and Label Stack Object Request flag and the G flag. The responder SHOULD then return a Detailed Interface and Label Stack TLV with an Incoming Interface Index Sub-TLV naming the LAG member link that received the request.

The initiator then sends one echo request per member link. In the success case, the requests reach the next router on two different member links. In the error case, both arrive on the same link, or one or both do not arrive at all.

The second way applies when Remote Interface Index sub-TLVs are available. The downstream router compares its incoming member link with the interface index in the DDMAP, and a mismatch results in the return code "Downstream Mapping Mismatch (5)".

These checks are deterministic only for LAGs connected back to back. If an L2 switch sits in between, the appendix explains that the sender may have no way to know which link a packet really traversed, and the suggested remedy is to try many entropy labels and see what comes back. Because exercising many links sends many echo messages in a short time, implementations are RECOMMENDED to randomly delay requests and replies to avoid congestion.
sections.eli5: The tester sends one message down each wire and asks the router at the other end which wire it arrived on. If two messages arrive on the same wire, something is wrong.

sections.title: The New TLVs and Sub-TLVs
sections.content:
The RFC defines these new formats, each starting with a 2-octet Type and a 2-octet Length:

  • Local Interface Index Sub-TLV: Type 4, Length 4, carrying the interface index the local router assigned to an egress interface.
  • Remote Interface Index Sub-TLV: Type 5, Length 4, optional, carrying the index a downstream router assigned to an ingress interface.
  • Detailed Interface and Label Stack TLV: Type 6, derived from the Interface and Label Stack TLV of RFC 8029, with the label stack turned into a sub-TLV. It may appear in an echo reply, at most once.

Inside the Detailed Interface and Label Stack TLV, two sub-TLVs are defined: Incoming Label Stack (sub-type 1), holding the labels as received with any changed TTL values restored (SHOULD), and Incoming Interface Index (sub-type 2, Length 8). The latter has an Interface Index Flags field in which the M flag marks the index as a member of a LAG.

The Address Type field in the TLV distinguishes IPv4 Numbered, IPv4 Unnumbered, IPv6 Numbered and IPv6 Unnumbered interfaces, with values 1 to 4.
sections.eli5: These are new labelled boxes in the message: one for 'my number for this wire', one for 'your number for this wire', and one for 'where the message came in'.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
These are on-demand diagnostic tools used by an operator inside an MPLS control domain. RFC 8029 reviews the possible attacks and mitigations, and this RFC relies on that analysis.

To prevent leakage of vital information to untrusted users, a responder MUST accept MPLS echo requests only from designated trusted sources, by filtering the source IP address. The RFC admits this is only a weak form of access control and not generally a reliable security mechanism, but says it is required in the absence of anything more robust.
sections.eli5: A router should only answer test messages from people it trusts, because the answers reveal how the network is built.
